constitutive_assumptions: Hooke's law governs the mechanical response and axial tension of the twisted multi-strand cable with an elastic coefficient k.
All mechanical work input by the motor torque is converted entirely into elastic potential energy of the cable without energy losses.
Equal-volume cylinder deformation assumption (V0 = Vtwisted) was evaluated and identified as inaccurate for multi-strand cables due to inter-strand gap closure during initial twisting.
The multi-substrate continuum assembly behaves as an equivalent cantilever beam with a modified structural stiffness coefficient (adjusted from 3 to 2) to account for discrete matrix interactions.
Circumferential drive cables behave elastically as linear spring elements under tensile load.

Tribological contact between spherical concave-convex substrates follows Coulomb friction, with maximum static friction torque proportional to normal contact force and contact radius (Mf = mu * N * Rcontact).
Worst-case minimum base stiffness assumes the continuum bends such that only a single drive cable sustains tensile force.
control_variables: Substrate dimensions and geometry (total length 295 mm, convex substrate length 15 mm, concave substrate length 20 mm, cross-sectional radius 5 mm)
Joint substrate allocation (6 substrates in joint 1, 6 in joint 2, 5 in joint 3)
Repetition count (5 experimental trials averaged per data point)
Failure criterion definition (end displacement exceeding 250 mm or motor torque limit reached)

evidence_relevant_to_topic.claim: Continuum robots suffer from low inherent stiffness, especially under high aspect ratio conditions, which limits their payload capacity and manipulation precision.

Twisting multi-strand cables generates axial contraction force and tension significantly greater than conventional linear cable pulling, offering higher normal force for inter-segment friction locking.
Axial shortening of twisted cables conflicts with the fixed structural length of continuum bodies, necessitating an axial retraction compensation mechanism.
A concave-convex-concave spherical interface contact between adjacent substrates converts line contact into spherical surface contact, optimizing normal pressure transmission and friction generation.

An energy-balance-based contraction model accounts for initial inter-strand gap filling and predicts cable retraction significantly more accurately than an equal-volume cylinder model at higher rotation turns.

Under a 2 N radial load, the average stiffness increased by 127% (from 13.47 N/m to 31.5 N/m) and maximum load capacity increased by 231% (from 4.2 N to 13.9 N) using a 4-strand configuration at 15 motor turns.

A three-strand cable configuration exhibits more uniform torsional transmission and concentrated tension distribution than two-strand or four-strand arrangements due to symmetric equilateral triangle packing.

experimental_setup: Resin-fabricated 3-joint bionic spine-like continuum robot prototype (17 substrates total: 6 in joint 1, 6 in joint 2, 5 in joint 3; total length 295 mm, individual substrate lengths 15 mm convex and 20 mm concave, radius 5 mm).
Passive retraction mechanism consisting of a sleeve linked to the drive box and a 4-groove slider with locking bolts to accommodate TSA cable shortening.
Twisted Multi-String Actuator unit utilizing Vectran cables (2-strand, 3-strand, and 4-strand) driven by a dedicated torsion motor and shaft coupling.
Cable retraction test platform measuring contraction length Delta L across varying motor torsion turns N.

Variable stiffness loading test bench configuring the robot as a horizontal cantilever beam, applying radial end loads using calibrated weights (0.5 N increments) while monitoring displacement and cable tension via a dynamometer.
future_work: Develop fully automated, dynamic retraction mechanisms to enable real-time and continuous variable stiffness modulation.
Integrate embedded pose and tension sensors for closed-loop stiffness control.
Explore alternative TSA cable routing and deployment topologies to expand robot workspace and bending curvature range.
Incorporate higher-torque actuation units to further expand load-bearing capacity.
Investigate robot dynamic interaction performance and stability during operational tasks.
independent_variables: Number of motor torsion turns (N: up to 30 turns for n=2 and n=3; up to 17 turns for retraction and 15 turns for stiffness tests for n=4)
External radial load applied at the end-effector (F: 0 to ~14 N in 0.5 N increments)
limitations_inferred: Manual loosening and tightening of slider bolts during retraction prevents continuous, in-motion stiffness adaptation during dynamic robotic tasks.
Repeated friction locking between 3D-printed resin spherical interfaces may result in progressive surface wear, changing the friction coefficient over extended cyclic loading.
Static dead-weight loading does not capture dynamic viscoelastic relaxation, vibration damping, or hysteresis of the twisted Vectran cables under high-frequency interaction.
limitations_stated_by_authors: The passive retraction mechanism is not yet fully automated and requires manual loosening and re-tightening of bolts.
Vectran cable rupture occurs under loads greater than 20 N, constraining the safe experimental loading regime to 0-10 N.
Arranging the TSA cable along the central axis restricts the maximum substrate joint bending angle to between 11 and 13 degrees.
Central TSA cable routing provides lower routing flexibility compared to traditional single-cable force-locking schemes.
Stiffness modulation is constrained by the torque limits of the drive motors, causing substrate slippage when external load exceeds maximum friction force.
main_results: The bionic continuum robot achieved omnidirectional bending up to 90 degrees across all directions, validating motion feasibility with joint movement limits of 13 degrees (concave-convex) and 11 degrees (convex-concave).

The theoretical contraction model derived from virtual work/energy balance accurately matched measured multi-strand cable retraction, outperforming the traditional constant-volume model at higher torsion revolutions.

TSA actuation significantly enhanced structural stiffness; for n=4 strands at N=15 turns, average stiffness reached 31.5 N/m compared to 13.47 N/m in the unstiffened baseline (a 127% increase), and maximum failure load rose from 4.2 N to 13.9 N (a 231% increase).
For n=3 strands at N=30 turns, the maximum tolerable load increased by 135% (from 4.0 N to 9.4 N).

Structural failure consistently occurred at an end displacement of approximately 250 mm across all strand configurations, preceded by a slope change at roughly 150 mm indicating partial inter-substrate slip.

Symmetric packing in the 3-strand cable provided optimal torsional transmission uniformity compared to 2-strand (side-overloading tendency) and 4-strand (uneven gap and torque concentration) arrangements.
modeling_methods: Kinematic/geometric modeling of twisted string contraction (cylindrical expansion and helix angle formulation modified for radius expansion).
Energy balance and virtual work modeling of TSA contraction relating motor input torque to cable elastic strain energy.
Cantilever beam structural mechanics modeling with a discrete matrix correction factor (Krobot = 2 * Ebase * Ibase / l^3).
Tribological force-locking formulation deriving inter-substrate spherical contact friction torque from normal forces induced by TSA and drive cables.
Two-state mechanical equilibrium modeling distinguishing between pure static friction (relative rest) and post-slip partial inter-substrate rotation.
Geometric aperture constraint analysis for maximum inter-substrate bending and rotational limit angles.
performance_metrics: Average stiffness under load (N/m) and percentage stiffness increase (%)
Maximum tolerable load / failure load (N) and percentage load capacity increase (%)
possible_gap_implications: While central single-channel TSA integration enhances overall bending stiffness, exploring distributed or eccentric multi-TSA routing could enable decoupled multi-segment or direction-dependent stiffness tuning without sacrificing individual joint angular range.

Developing motorized or pneumatic auto-locking retraction slides is essential before TSA-based variable stiffness continuum manipulators can be applied in clinical or confined industrial environments.
paper.research_objective: To design, model, and experimentally evaluate a variable stiffness continuum robot utilizing Twisted Multi-String Actuators (TSA) integrated into a bionic spine-like configuration with a passive retraction mechanism, thereby expanding the stiffness adjustment range and payload capacity beyond traditional single-cable force-locking methods.
paper.research_problem: Continuum robots exhibit an inherent trade-off between high flexibility and low structural stiffness under high aspect ratios, while conventional variable-stiffness methods suffer from slow response, complex auxiliary systems, or narrow tuning ranges. Moreover, traditional single-cable force-locking is constrained by single-cable tension limits, and integrating TSA into continuum bodies introduces severe motion conflicts due to axial cable retraction against a fixed body length.
stiffness_mechanism: inter-substrate friction modulation via spherical contact interfaces
paper.title: Design Characteristics of Continuum Robots Based on TSA Variable Stiffness Method
